old: Its deepest root simply meant a sturdy prop or beam — nothing about height or views.
In Old Italian, the word first named a kind of scaffold before it ever meant a place to stand and look out.
It's a distant cousin of the English word 'balk,' both descending from a Germanic word for 'beam.'
clues: This part of a building began with an ancient root meaning 'beam, pile, prop,' and in Old Italian its ancestor meant 'scaffold.'
Unlike a patio or porch at ground level, it is a railed platform jutting from an upper floor, where apartment or hotel guests step out for air.
Juliet famously speaks from one in Shakespeare's play, and theaters use the word for their upper seating level. It shares its beam root with the English word 'balk.'
